content.title: About
content.content: The Breakfast Tart is a layered pastry typically made from buttery flaky dough filled with a light cream, berries, fruit, or nuts. It combines a crisp crust with a airy filling, making it an ideal dish for a morning meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tart originated in France in the 17th century as a "tarte" – an open‑top pie that later evolved into more elaborate versions.
Traditional breakfast tarts often feature seasonal berries such as raspberry or blueberry, giving them a bright flavor and aroma.
The flaky dough used in a tart contains a high amount of butter, which creates its characteristic golden colour and crunch.
Tarts can be sweet or savory; in some regions they are served with ham and cheese for a hearty start.
Japan has a similar dessert called "mochi‑tart," where the dough is replaced by a sticky rice cake.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The flaky pastry and cream provide carbohydrates and fats that quickly supply energy for the start of the day.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as eggs and dairy deliver vitamins B1, B2 and B12, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from berries
items.content: Fresh berries in the filling contain vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy components in the cream support bone and tooth health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When nuts or whole‑grain dough are added, the tart boosts fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The tart is rich in butter and sugar, so it should be enjoyed in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Allergy to dairy and eggs
items.content: The cream and dough often contain milk and eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet fillings can raise blood glucose levels, which is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of butter may cause discomfort for individuals with gallbladder disease or pancreatitis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the tart slightly warm or at room temperature. Cut it into portions and pair with coffee, tea, or fresh juice. Add a dollop of yogurt or a light fruit sauce for extra freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the tart in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Before serving, let it reach room temperature or gently warm in the oven for 5‑7 minutes to restore crust crispness. Freezing is not recommended as the pastry may lose its structure.

content.title: About
content.content: Port du Salut is a semi‑soft French cheese with an orange‑red rind, produced from cow’s milk in the Auvergne region. It has a creamy texture, a mild nutty‑butter flavor, and a distinctive aroma that deepens with aging.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese is named after the Port du Salut monastery where it was first made in the 19th century.
The characteristic orange rind is created by adding a natural paprika‑derived coloring.
Often called the “monk’s cheese” because it was originally crafted by Benedictine monks.
The original recipe used only whole whey, but modern versions add cream for a smoother mouthfeel.
Port du Salut is typically served in small wedges to highlight its aroma.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Cow’s milk provides complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: During ripening beneficial bacteria develop, contributing to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low lactose content
items.content: Most lactose is drained with the whey, making the cheese often tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may react to the cheese.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Port du Salut contains a notable amount of salt; those with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Like most cheeses, it is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Biogenic amines
items.content: Extended aging can lead to histamine and tyramine formation, which may trigger reactions in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Port du Salut can be enjoyed on its own, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, casseroles, and pasta dishes. It melts well, making it suitable for fondue and baked recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment paper inside an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, re‑wrap in wax paper to prevent drying. It keeps best for 4‑6 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn is a cereal grain cultivated worldwide. Raw corn consists of whole ears that can be eaten after removing the husk and silk. It has a mildly sweet flavor, crunchy texture, and provides carbohydrates, fiber, and various vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn originated in Central and South America, where it was domesticated over 7,000 years ago.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, ranging in kernel color from yellow and white to red, blue, and even black.
Corn is a staple food in many countries and appears in traditional dishes such as polenta, tamales, and corn chowder.
Corn ears can grow taller than 3 meters (10 feet).
Raw corn contains antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin that are beneficial for eye health.

items.title: Rich source of energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy and help maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes regular bowel movements, and can aid in cholesterol management.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Raw corn supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Eye‑protecting antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect the eyes from UV damage and may reduce the risk of age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Corn provides magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for muscle function and fluid balance.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop a corn allergy, resulting in skin rashes, swelling, or respiratory issues.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Raw corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or sprouting lowers its level.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth producing aflatoxins, so proper storage conditions are essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw corn can be enjoyed as fresh ears cut into bite‑size pieces and added to salads, salsas, or smoothies. It can also be boiled, steamed, or grilled. Soaking the kernels for a few hours softens them for easier chewing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ears in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container, where they stay crisp for up to 5 days. Frozen corn kernels should be stored in an airtight bag at –18 °C (0 °F) and retain quality for 8‑12 months. Discard any ears with off‑odors or visible mold.
